tip: Spanish can shrink a whole if-clause into two words, 'de' + infinitive: 'de haber tenido tiempo' = 'if I had had time' – no 'si', no subject, common in writing.
Where English pulls legs, Spanish grabs hair: 'no me tomes el pelo' = 'don't take my hair', i.e. stop teasing me. Same joke, different body part.
'De tal palo, tal astilla' is carpentry: a splinter ('astilla') carved off a stick ('palo') is the same wood – just as 'el hijo' is cut from 'el padre'.
'Una canguro' is literally 'a kangaroo' – Spain's everyday word for a babysitter. Latin America uses 'niñera' instead.
Why 'saldremos', not 'saliremos'? The future dropped the 'i' of 'salir', and the leftover 'salr-' was awkward, so Spanish wedged in a 'd' as a bridge: 'sal-d-remos'.
'Podremos' isn't 'poder' + '-emos': the future drops the 'e' of 'poder', leaving 'podr-'. 'Saber' and 'haber' do the same – 'sabr-', 'habr-'.
'Pase lo que pase' is literally 'may it happen what may happen'. The doubled subjunctive means 'no matter what' – the statement holds whatever the outcome.
Imperfect for a habitual past: 'nos peleábamos' = we used to fight.
'Estaría' here isn't polite 'would be' – with 'según él' it's the reporting conditional: 'is supposedly ready'. Spanish news uses it to flag unconfirmed claims.
Spanish centuries skip 'fifteenth': 'el siglo quince' is literally 'century fifteen'. Past the tenth century, ordinals get clunky, so plain numbers usually take over.
English needs two 'the's (the sooner, the better); Spanish drops both: 'cuanto antes lo terminemos, mejor' – and the not-yet-done verb goes subjunctive ('terminemos').
'Se oyen' is plural because 'risas' is the grammatical subject – literally 'laughters hear themselves'. With this 'se', the thing heard controls the verb: 'se oyen risas'.
'Domine' is subjunctive because this spreadsheet wizard may not exist yet – 'alguien que' + subjunctive describes a wish list, not a real person you've already found.
'Cuyas' means whose (feminine plural): 'cuyo' agrees in gender and number with the noun it precedes, not the owner.
Two 'buts' in Spanish: after a negation that corrects, 'pero' gives way to 'sino' – 'no es cuestión de suerte, sino de decisión' ('not X but rather Y').
Why 'sea', not 'es'? Unknown things take the subjunctive: 'lo que sea necesario' = whatever turns out to be necessary. 'Lo que es' would mean you already know what that is.
Future perfect for past guessing: '¿Qué habrá pasado?' means 'what could have happened?' – you're guessing about a past event.
'For the park'? No – 'por el parque' means through/around it. 'Por' marks movement inside a space: 'caminar por' = wander through, not walk for.
Where's 'each other'? Packed into 'nos': 'nos veremos' = we'll see each other. Spanish reuses reflexive pronouns for 'each other' too – context decides which.
Don't add 'for' – 'pedir' already means ask for: 'pedir un aumento' = ask for a raise. 'Pedir por' exists, but it means to plead on someone's behalf.
English strands prepositions ('cousins we played with'); Spanish never does. 'Con' jumps up front: 'los primos con los que jugábamos' – preposition + article + 'que'.
'Hubiera hecho' (past condition) + 'tendríamos' (present result) = a mixed conditional.
'Con tal de que' is literally 'with such (a condition) that' = as long as. It names a condition, so subjunctive follows: 'con tal de que seas feliz'.
'Ni pies ni cabeza' is literally 'neither feet nor head' = it makes no sense. Where English can't make head or tail of something, Spanish says it's missing both ends.
Why 'están', not 'son'? Closed is the windows' current state – the result of someone shutting them. 'Estar' + participle = resulting condition: 'están cerradas'.
Two pasts, one line: 'llovía' (imperfect) sets the ongoing background; 'llegamos' (preterite) is the completed event that happened against it.
'Habrás oído' looks future but aims backward: with 'seguro que ya', it's a confident bet about the past – 'you'll have heard it' meaning 'I'm sure you already have.'
No subjunctive after 'creo que'! Affirmative belief asserts something real: 'creo que lloverá'. Only the negative flips it: 'no creo que llueva'.
For 'yet', Spanish reuses 'still': 'todavía no he comido' is literally 'still I haven't eaten' = I haven't eaten yet.
'En cuanto' + subjunctive for future events: 'tenga' (not 'tengo').
